knowledge_point.title: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating

question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-(x + 3)-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-(x + 3)}{e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-(x + 3)} \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-(x + 3)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{-(x + 3)}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =-{e}^{-(x + 3)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{-(x + 3)}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{-(x + 3)}+C).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(-3)=0$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-3) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{0}+C) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(C-1) & =0 \\ C-1 & =1 \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{-(x + 3)-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(-3)=0$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-{e}^{-(x + 3)}).
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the specific solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{-2(x + 1)-y}$ given that  $\,y(-1)=2.$

$y(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡($
{{field-1}} $)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-2(x + 1)-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-2(x + 1)}{e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-2(x + 1)} \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-2(x + 1)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{-2(x + 1)}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2(x + 1)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2(x + 1)}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2(x + 1)}+C).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(-1)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-1) & =2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{0}+C) & =2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(C-\frac{1}{2}) & =2 \\ C-\frac{1}{2} & ={e}^{2} \\ C & =\frac{2{e}^{2}+1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{-2(x + 1)-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(-1)=2$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{-{e}^{-2(x + 1)}+2{e}^{2}+1}{2}\right).
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the nonconstant local solution to $y'=2(x + 3)\sqrt{1-y^2}$ by separating variables. Work on a local branch where the sine argument $\theta$ satisfies $-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2$. Express the solution as $y=\sin(\boxed{\text{expression}}+C)$.

Expression: {{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x + 3)\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x + 3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2(x + 3)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arcsin}⁡y & ={(x + 3)}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

This is a perfectly valid general solution. However, if we want to write $y=y(x)$ explicitly, then we can solve for $y.$ This gives

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡({(x + 3)}^{2}+C)
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

This nonconstant branch applies where $-\pi/2<(x + 3)^2+C<\pi/2$, so $\cos((x + 3)^2+C)>0$. The constant endpoint solutions $y=\pm1$ also solve the ODE.

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{(x - 3)}^{2}}+{y}^{2}$ that satisfies $y(2)=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{(x - 3)}^{2}}+{y}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{(x - 3)}^{2}}+1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{{(x - 3)}^{2}}+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{{(x - 3)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =-\frac{1}{(x - 3)}+(x - 3)+C \\ \frac{1}{y} & =\frac{1-{(x - 3)}^{2}-C(x - 3)}{(x - 3)} \\ y & =\frac{(x - 3)}{1-{(x - 3)}^{2}-C(x - 3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{(x - 3)}{1-{(x - 3)}^{2}-C(x - 3)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(2)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & =1 \\ \frac{-1}{1-(-1)^{2}-C(-1)} & =1 \\ \frac{-1}{C} & =1 \\ C & =-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{(x - 3)}^{2}}+{y}^{2}$ that satisfies the condition $y(2)=1$ is

$$
y=\frac{(x - 3)}{1+(x - 3)-{(x - 3)}^{2}}\,.
$$
